PullRequest.Title: Refactor Markdown rich editor messaging to HubRPC
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary
Replace the Markdown rich editor extension/webview message switches with typed, runtime-validated `@vscode/hubrpc` interfaces.

- Preserve the authoritative `TextDocument`, edit epochs, undo/redo ordering, and existing editor behavior.
- Authenticate each webview generation and close requests/listeners on reload or disposal.
- Cover document synchronization, commands, highlighting, comments, rich links, and embedded-editor routing.
- Keep source-editing changes, local package overrides, rename/suggest widgets, and diagnostics out of scope.

## Validation
- 28 targeted extension tests passed, including 7 RPC/bridge regressions.
- Extension compilation, renderer typecheck/build, and browser extension bundle passed.
- Targeted ESLint and precommit hygiene passed.
- User verified Code OSS with the migrated editor before extraction.

The isolated branch uses the published Markdown editor dependency. The standard gulp bootstrap encountered an unrelated shared Copilot runtime mismatch; the exact `compile-extension:markdown-language-features` task passed when loaded directly from `build/gulpfile.extensions.ts`.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The per-edit call path, serialized host queue, discarded Promise result, and old one-way behavior are all explicit in the diff. Exact millisecond cost varies by platform and typing rate, but the 2x boundary-message count and backlog-proportional pending requests are deterministic.
Findings.PerformanceResource: webview/extension-host IPC messages, client-side pending-request entries, and Promise objects
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Each source-text change creates one JSON-RPC request and one response, so typing N edits now causes 2N cross-boundary messages and retains N request completions until the serialized WorkspaceEdit queue catches up; the same pattern also affects the bidirectional embedded-editor message stream.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: excessive IPC and allocation/GC pressure on continuous typing or chatty embedded-editor sessions, reducing extension-host/webview throughput
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The renderer posted each edit as a one-way webview message. The extension host enqueued the WorkspaceEdit, but no acknowledgement crossed back to the webview and no client request remained pending.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: `edit` is now declared as `requestType(..., z.void())`. `Editor` invokes it from the source-text autorun for every local edit and immediately discards the returned result through `#send`; HubRPC must still correlate the request and send a void response after the host's serialized edit completes.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 66 changes the edit event to `requestType(..., z.void())`; deleted editor/provider hunks show the prior one-way `postMessage({ type: 'edit', ... })` path, while added editor.ts lines 483-486 call the request from the text-change autorun without consuming a result.
Findings.Title: Keep per-keystroke edits on a one-way channel
Findings.Impact: Typing in the rich Markdown editor generates an otherwise-unused response for every keystroke. If WorkspaceEdit processing falls behind input, pending RPC promises grow with the backlog, while nested editor transport messages declared the same way can further amplify the webview/extension-host traffic.
Findings.Evidence: The changed source-text autorun calls `this.#host.edit(...)` for every text change, while the handler awaits `editQueue.enqueue`, whose tasks serialize `workspace.applyEdit`. HubRPC tests added in this PR explicitly verify request correlation and rejection of pending calls on close, confirming that even void methods are tracked requests. The deleted implementation used one `postMessage` per edit with no response path.
Findings.Recommendation: Use a typed one-way notification for `edit` (and the two `codeBlockEditorHostTransportMessage` event streams), preserving transport ordering and the existing host-side edit queue. Keep request/response only for operations whose result or completion is actually consumed, such as ready barriers, history, and code-block resolution.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The recursive schema, receive path, token-array shape, per-edit request frequency, and post-response stale check are directly visible in changed code. Payload sizes vary by document, affecting severity but not the extra O(payload-size) mechanism.
Findings.PerformanceResource: CPU work and temporary arrays/objects produced while validating full JSON payload trees
Findings.PerformanceScaling: The added `z.json()` checks traverse payloads by total nested value count. Highlight responses contain one object per syntax token, so the added work is O(token count) for every completed request, including stale responses from rapid edits; opaque embedded-editor payloads scale with their full message size as well.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased webview/extension-host CPU and GC pressure, delaying syntax-highlight updates and increasing typing jank for large or frequently edited fenced code blocks
Findings.PreviousBehavior: The previous authenticated message switch checked message type/IDs and passed highlight token arrays or opaque embedded-editor payloads directly to their consumers; stale highlighting results were rejected by the highlighter without first running a generic recursive JSON parse.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Every received JSON-RPC request/result/error now goes through `rpcMessage.safeParse`, whose `params`, `result`, and `error.data` use recursive `z.json()` schemas. HubRPC then applies the method-specific schemas such as `highlightResult`, so large payloads are traversed generically before the authoritative interface validation and before request-version stale-result checks.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added line 17 defines all RPC results as `z.json()`; added lines 42-46 run `rpcMessage.safeParse` before dispatch, and the new protocol separately defines the token-array `highlightResult` validator used by the highlight request.
Findings.Title: Avoid recursively parsing RPC payloads in the transport
Findings.Impact: Opening, editing, or theme-refreshing Markdown with large fenced code blocks returns large token arrays. Rapid edits can leave multiple full-highlighting requests in flight; each stale result still pays the newly added full-tree parse before `HighlighterDocument` discards it, wasting CPU and allocations on the rendering path.
Findings.Evidence: `MarkdownEditorRpcTransport` calls `rpcMessage.safeParse` before forwarding any message. The new highlight result schema is an array of token objects, `HighlighterDocument.update` requests full highlighting on every code-block edit, and staleness is checked only after awaiting the RPC result. The protocol's method-specific `highlightResult` schema already provides runtime validation.
Findings.Recommendation: Validate only the JSON-RPC envelope shape in `MarkdownEditorRpcTransport` (protocol version, id, method, and presence of params/result/error), leaving payloads as unknown for HubRPC's method-specific runtime schemas. This preserves authentication and typed validation while removing the redundant full-tree traversal.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open or reload a rich Markdown editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The webview HTML must load, construct the RPC connection and editor, send `ready`, and receive any authoritative document replacement before initialization settles. Provider/comment/diff publication follows readiness. The embedded-editor adapter dynamic import is off this path unless a fenced block is rendered while providers exist.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Authenticated webview-to-extension-host `ready` request and extension-host-to-webview initialization requests
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One ready exchange per webview generation, plus at most one initial publication each for provider/comment/diff state when available
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Equivalent initialization crossed the webview boundary through one-way messages; the PR replaces the protocol and adds responses for void RPC methods.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Ready handling gates resynchronization and publication of initial renderer state.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dynamic import of the embedded-editor adapter chunk
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most once per editor factory, and only after a fenced block is requested while providers exist
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The adapter was statically imported and bundled/evaluated with the main editor path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off initial editor startup; it blocks only first embedded-editor creation and ordinary code-block rendering remains available meanwhile.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Document size controls initial content transfer; provider, comment, and diff collections control initial payload sizes. The lazy adapter load is independent of fenced-block count after the first trigger.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One RPC connection per webview generation. Initial contribution loading may complete before or after ready but publication is readiness-gated; reload uses a serialized edit-queue barrier.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The editor starts from embedded initial document state. Code-block provider definitions and existing resolved-editor caches are reused until contribution/trust changes clear them; the dynamic adapter module is loaded once per webview factory.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the changed critical path and deferred adapter load from direct constructor and ready-handler tracing.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: HubRPC/Zod startup bundle and schema-registration costs were not benchmarked, and document/provider collection sizes vary.
Scenarios.Verdict: The lazy adapter improves startup placement, while RPC initialization adds bounded overhead. No additional opening-path regression beyond the reported generic RPC parsing and request/response mechanisms was established.

Scenarios.Scenario: Type continuously in the rich Markdown editor
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each model source-text change computes a text edit, sends it to the extension host, enters `RecoveringTaskQueue`, and performs `workspace.applyEdit`; the local renderer does not wait for the returned Promise, but HubRPC retains and acknowledges each request.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: JSON-RPC edit request from webview plus void result response
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One request and one response per effective source-text change/keystroke; N edits produce 2N cross-boundary messages and N pending request completions while the host queue drains
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Each edit used one one-way webview message; host WorkspaceEdit processing was already serialized but generated no response and retained no client RPC request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Local rendering is optimistic, but host synchronization, history barriers, extension-host load, and pending-request lifetime scale with the edit backlog.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Apply a WorkspaceEdit to the authoritative TextDocument
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One application per accepted current-epoch edit, serialized globally for this editor
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same per-edit WorkspaceEdit and serialization existed before the RPC refactor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Must complete before the next queued edit and before undo/redo or link-opening barriers progress.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Typing/input event count after model updates; effective cardinality is one accepted edit per source-text change, not per document character.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Host edits are strictly serialized by `RecoveringTaskQueue`; webview requests can arrive concurrently and accumulate as pending RPCs while that queue drains. There is no edit coalescing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache serves edits. Epoch invalidation drops stale queued work after authoritative replacement, but current-epoch edits and their RPC completions remain individually tracked.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high; the autorun, request declaration, serialized queue, and discarded client result are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual backlog depends on WorkspaceEdit latency and typing/bulk-input rate, but the doubled boundary-message count is deterministic.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable boundary fan-out: a previously one-way per-keystroke event is now request/response RPC.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render, edit, or theme-refresh fenced code-block syntax highlighting
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each live fenced block requests full syntax highlighting from the extension host. The response must cross the webview boundary and be parsed before the latest result updates tokens; stale results are discarded only after RPC completion.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send code-block source to `computeFullSyntaxHighlighting` and return the token/color arrays
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One request per code-block creation and update; a theme change fans out one request per live block. Rapid edits may have multiple requests in flight because only result application, not computation, is version-suppressed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same full-highlighting request/result boundary existed through custom messages.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The latest response gates styled token rendering; stale responses are off the useful critical path but still consume host, IPC, and parse work.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively validate the complete JSON-RPC result with `z.json()` before HubRPC method-specific result validation
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One full payload-tree traversal for every result received, including each stale highlight result; token cardinality scales with highlighted source/token runs
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The custom authenticated message switch forwarded token arrays directly; it did not generically recurse through every result payload before the highlighter's stale check.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs before the response reaches the request-version check, directly delaying useful results and wasting work for stale results.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of live fenced blocks, code-block source length/token count, edit frequency, and theme-change fan-out.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Highlight calls are unconstrained across blocks and updates; request versions suppress stale application but do not cancel in-flight host computation, transport, or parsing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No result cache or request coalescing is present. Each block retains its latest tokens; every edit and theme change requests a full result.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high for the parse path and fan-out; exact jank depends on block size and edit cadence.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Token density and language-service duration vary by language and file, but O(total returned tokens) redundant parsing and stale-result reachability are direct.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable serialization/allocation regression from generic recursive payload parsing before method validation.

Scenarios.Scenario: Create and exchange messages with embedded fenced-code editors
Scenarios.CriticalPath: On first eligible block, the adapter chunk loads; provider resolution may cross RPC; host-transport messages then flow bidirectionally between nested iframe, webview, and extension host. First editor creation waits for adapter loading and provider resolution, while later traffic is event-driven.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Load the web-editors adapter via dynamic import
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per rich-editor webview after the first eligible block; shared module loading may be warm after prior loads
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Adapter code was statically included/eagerly evaluated with the main editor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Blocks only first embedded-editor creation; normal fenced-block rendering continues while loading.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve an exported code-block provider descriptor
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Per provider/language cache miss as selected by the adapter; existing resolved-editor caches reduce repeated host/provider work
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: An explicit request ID and response message performed the same round trip.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before the corresponding embedded editor can be created.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Route opaque host-transport payloads in both directions as void JSON-RPC requests and acknowledgements
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One request plus one response per nested-editor transport event in either direction; scales with aggregate traffic across live embedded editors
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Each opaque payload was forwarded as a one-way postMessage with no acknowledgement.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Payload delivery is on nested-editor interaction/model-sync paths; acknowledgements are unused but consume boundary and request-tracking capacity.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively parse opaque nested JSON payloads through the generic RPC `z.json()` envelope schema
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One traversal per received payload, scaling with its complete nested size
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Opaque messages were routed after only checking type/runtime ID and were not recursively traversed by a generic JSON schema.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs before transport payload delivery to the nested editor/provider.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of eligible blocks/live runtimes, provider/language combinations after cache reuse, and per-runtime message rate/payload size.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Adapter loading is single-flight per factory. Provider resolution and messages can run across multiple live runtimes without a shared limiter; each runtime has independent transport state.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Lazy factory load is single-shot. Existing provider descriptor/resource caches are cleared on contribution/trust changes; failures are not retried until editor reopen. Runtime messages are not cached or coalesced.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High from protocol declarations, call sites, transport parser, and old one-way deleted paths.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Nested provider protocols differ in message rate and payload size; this lowers certainty of user-visible magnitude but not the introduced 2x message shape or recursive parse.
Scenarios.Verdict: The lazy adapter placement is beneficial. The request/response and recursive parsing costs share the two reported root causes, so no duplicate finding was submitted.

Scenarios.Scenario: Update rich links, comments, and diff markers
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Renderer target changes synchronize the current deduplicated href set to the host; each new href resolves and creates one presentation watcher. Comment/diff provider events serialize their current collections and publish them after ready.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Synchronize the deduplicated rich-link target set and publish individual presentations
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Target-set sends are microtask-coalesced per synchronous render turn; one resolver/watcher per distinct href, with presentation updates per watcher event
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Equivalent target sets and presentation updates crossed one-way messages; void RPC now adds acknowledgements but effective target cardinality is unchanged.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off document editing progress; it gates rich presentation updates only.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve/open rich-link resources through configured link resolvers/watchers, which may reach remote providers depending on rule
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most once per distinct live href initialization plus watcher-specific updates; duplicate hrefs share one entry
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same per-distinct-href resolver and watcher lifecycle existed before the bridge refactor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off core editor readiness and typing; only rich-link decoration waits.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Publish complete comments or gutter-marker collections to the webview
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One collection publication per provider/document change after readiness, plus one on each webview ready generation
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Equivalent full collections were posted through the previous message switch.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off text editing critical path; required only for ancillary decorations.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct live href count after deduplication, comment count, changed-line range count, and provider event frequency.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Rich-link target synchronization coalesces within one microtask but does not wait for an earlier request; per-href initialization runs independently. Diff computation can overlap document events but version checks reject stale results.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Rich-link entries are reference-counted and removed at zero references; duplicate hrefs share watchers. Diff providers maintain their own current state and stale/version checks. No new unbounded cache was found.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for grouping, readiness gates, and lifecycle from the controller/provider code.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Remote resolver behavior depends on installed link providers, but that boundary and cardinality are pre-existing.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate performance regression: collection cardinality and expensive resolution behavior are preserved, while generic RPC overhead is already covered by the reported root causes.

Scenarios.Scenario: Dispose or reload a rich editor generation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Reload serializes behind accepted edits, disposes embedded host transports, closes the old RPC connection/listener, creates a new authenticated generation, and reconfigures HTML. Panel disposal cancels provider work and tears down listeners/maps.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Close pending RPC requests and detach webview listeners during reset/disposal
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Once per reload generation or panel disposal; pending requests are rejected/aborted as a group by connection close
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The previous bridge disposed its direct listener and resolved pending code-block requests manually; it lacked a general RPC pending-request set.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Reload waits for the edit barrier before reset; panel disposal does not wait for remote acknowledgements.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of pending requests and live embedded runtimes at reload/disposal.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Reload is ordered by an edit-queue barrier; connection close aborts in-flight handlers and detaches the transport subscription. Disposal is idempotent.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Per-generation pending messages and listeners are cleared; embedded runtime maps are disposed; no unbounded retained generation state was found.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High; reset/close/dispose paths and tests establish cleanup behavior.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Reload frequency and pending-request count vary, but cleanup ownership is explicit and tested.
Scenarios.Verdict: No cleanup-lifecycle regression found; the new connection and transport are closed on both reload and disposal.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 17 changed files and all diff pages. Reported two introduced regressions: request/response fan-out for fire-and-forget hot event streams, and redundant recursive JSON payload parsing on large/stale RPC results. Traced startup, typing, highlighting, embedded editors, rich-link/comment/diff updates, and generation cleanup; no additional high-confidence performance issues or qualifying regression fix were found.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
